title: Quiet good
hook: Amar Das carries river water before dawn for Guru Angad, falls in a storm and is mocked as homeless: Sikh seva, good with the ego out of the way
tomorrow: a Zen herder finally catches the ox. where does he go next?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: speak up, when your conscience is clear. Some good has to be loud. Today, the other kind.

Cold water on your hands. The weight of a full pitcher. A river you can hear but not see. Sikh tradition tells of an old man who knew all three. Amar Das came to the second Guru, Guru Angad, late in life. Every day, before dawn, he walked to the river Beas, filled a pitcher, and carried the water back for the Guru's bath. No one asked him to. Hardly anyone saw him go.
screen: `COLD WATER, A FULL PITCHER.` → `AMAR DAS AT THE RIVER.` → `BEFORE DAWN, UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: Then one stormy night, rain and wind and no light, he tripped near a weaver's house and fell, holding the pitcher so the water wouldn't spill. The weaver's wife, woken by the noise, grumbled that it must be Amru, the homeless one, out wandering. The words reached Guru Angad. He answered that Amar Das was not homeless: he was the home of the homeless. In time, the tradition says, Guru Angad chose him to be the next Guru. The water carrier became the third Guru of the Sikhs. Under the story is seva: selfless service, done without wanting credit. Sikhs practice it in the gurdwara, washing dishes in the free kitchen, sweeping, and cleaning the shoes left at the door, without anyone needing to know who did it. The Guru Granth Sahib says that one who serves without desire for reward finds the Lord. The point isn't secrecy for its own sake. It's that the ego steps out of the way. Seva done in order to be seen has quietly turned into something else.
screen: `A FALL IN THE STORM.` · `AMRU THE HOMELESS.` · `THE HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · `SEVA: SERVICE WITHOUT REWARD.` · then, large: `QUIET GOOD.`

segments.voice: Stand, cup your hands in front of you as if they held a full pitcher, and walk slowly across the room and back without spilling a drop. As you walk, choose one small good you could do this week that no one will see or thank you for. Then sit, hands resting, until the bell.
Quiet good: seva, service with the ego out of the way, like Amar Das carrying the Guru's water before anyone woke.
Your line: quiet good. Amar Das carried the water in the dark, and the Guru heard anyway. That's day 1733.

screen: `DAY 1733 COUNTS.` → `IN THE WORLD · 13 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: A ZEN HERDER FINALLY CATCHES THE OX. WHERE DOES HE GO NEXT?`

howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara: cooking and washing up in the langar, sweeping, and looking after the shoes of the congregation. The story of Amar Das carrying water for Guru Angad is told as a picture of humble service.
